title: Metabolism & Bioenergetics
description: Free energy and ATP, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, pyruvate dehydrogenase, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, the pentose phosphate pathway, glycogen, fatty acids, the urea cycle and metabolic regulation.

cards.title: Which equation gives the actual free energy change $\Delta G$ of a reaction from $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ and the mass-action ratio $Q$?
cards.body:
$\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + RT\ln Q$

At equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K'_{eq}$, which gives $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT\ln K'_{eq}$.

Why: $\Delta G$ decides the direction under cellular conditions; $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ only describes the standard state.
Watch out: a reaction with a positive $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ can still run forward if $Q$ is small enough.
cards.searchQuery: delta G equals delta G standard prime plus RT ln Q

cards.title: What conditions define the biochemical standard state used for $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$?
cards.body:
pH $7.0$, $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1\,\mathrm{M}$ for all solutes and $1\,\mathrm{atm}$ for gases, with water taken as $1$ (its concentration is absorbed into the constant).

The prime means $[\ce{H+}] = 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{M}$ rather than $1\,\mathrm{M}$ as in chemistry's standard state.

Watch out: real cells have very different concentrations, so $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ is a reference value, not what happens in the cell.
cards.searchQuery: biochemical standard state pH 7 delta G naught prime

cards.title: A reaction has $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +5.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($RT = 2.48\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$). What is $K'_{eq}$, to the nearest power of ten? (number only)
cards.body:
0.1

$\ln K'_{eq} = -\dfrac{5.7}{2.48} = -2.3$, so $K'_{eq} = e^{-2.3} \approx 0.1$.

Key idea: a positive $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ means $K'_{eq} < 1$, so reactants are favored at equilibrium.
Tip: at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, every $5.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ of $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ changes $K'_{eq}$ by a factor of $10$.
cards.searchQuery: standard free energy change to equilibrium constant positive delta G

cards.title: What is the standard free energy of ATP hydrolysis to ADP + $\mathrm{P_i}$, $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$, in kJ/mol? (number with sign)
cards.body:
-30.5

The value is about $-7.3\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$. Inside cells, with ATP high and ADP and $\mathrm{P_i}$ low, the actual $\Delta G$ is more negative, about $-50$ to $-65\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Why: ATP is kept far from equilibrium, which makes it a strong driver of coupled reactions.
cards.searchQuery: ATP hydrolysis standard free energy -30.5 kJ/mol

cards.title: Why does ATP hydrolysis release so much free energy?
cards.body:
Products are more stable than ATP, for three reasons:

- Relief of electrostatic repulsion among the negative charges on the phosphate chain
- Better resonance stabilization of the released $\mathrm{P_i}$ (and of ADP)
- Stronger solvation of the products

Watch out: the "high-energy bond" is a misnomer; the energy comes from the whole reaction, not from the bond breaking by itself.
cards.searchQuery: why ATP hydrolysis releases energy charge repulsion resonance stabilization

cards.title: Which has the largest standard free energy of hydrolysis: PEP, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, creatine phosphate or ATP?
cards.body:
Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)

Approximate $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ of hydrolysis in kJ/mol: PEP $-61.9$, 1,3-BPG $-49.3$, creatine phosphate $-43.1$, ATP $-30.5$, glucose 6-phosphate $-13.8$.

Why: PEP releases enol-to-keto tautomerization energy once the phosphate leaves, which is why pyruvate kinase can make ATP.
Key idea: ATP sits in the middle, so it can accept a phosphate from higher donors and donate to lower ones.
cards.searchQuery: phosphoenolpyruvate highest phosphoryl transfer potential

cards.title: Glucose + $\mathrm{P_i} \to$ G6P has $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +13.8$; ATP hydrolysis has $-30.5\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Find $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ for glucose + ATP $\to$ G6P + ADP (kJ/mol).
cards.body:
-16.7

Free energies of coupled reactions **add**: $+13.8 + (-30.5) = -16.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Why: the shared intermediate (the phosphoryl group) lets the favorable reaction pay for the unfavorable one.
Example: this is exactly what hexokinase does in step 1 of glycolysis.
cards.searchQuery: coupled reactions free energies add hexokinase glucose ATP G6P

cards.title: $\Delta E^{\circ\prime}$ for NADH $\to \tfrac{1}{2}\ce{O2}$ is $1.14\,\mathrm{V}$ ($n = 2$, $F = 96.5\,\mathrm{kJ/(V \cdot mol)}$). What is $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ in kJ/mol? (nearest integer)
cards.body:
-220

$\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -nF\Delta E^{\circ\prime} = -2 \times 96.5 \times 1.14 = -220\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Key idea: this is enough for the electron transport chain to pump protons for roughly $2.5$ ATP per NADH.
Watch out: do not forget $n$, the number of electrons transferred.
cards.searchQuery: delta G = -nF delta E NADH oxygen redox free energy

cards.title: Which direction do electrons flow between two redox couples, and what are the standard reduction potentials of $\ce{NAD+}/\mathrm{NADH}$ and $\tfrac12\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O}$?
cards.body:
Electrons flow from the couple with the **more negative** $E^{\circ\prime}$ to the **more positive** one.

$E^{\circ\prime}(\ce{NAD+}/\mathrm{NADH}) = -0.32\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^{\circ\prime}(\tfrac12\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O}) = +0.82\,\mathrm{V}$.

Why: NADH is a strong electron donor, and oxygen is a strong acceptor, so the whole chain runs downhill.
cards.searchQuery: standard reduction potential NAD+/NADH -0.32 oxygen +0.82

cards.title: Why are the regulated steps of a pathway almost always reactions that are far from equilibrium?
cards.body:
Their $\Delta G$ is large and negative ($Q \ll K'_{eq}$), so changing enzyme activity changes the pathway flux directly.

Near-equilibrium reactions simply follow substrate levels, and enzyme changes there have little effect on net flux.

Example: hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase are the far-from-equilibrium steps of glycolysis.
Key idea: **irreversible steps** are the control points.
cards.searchQuery: metabolic regulation far from equilibrium steps flux control

cards.title: Cells have $[\mathrm{ATP}]:[\mathrm{ADP}]:[\mathrm{AMP}]$ in the ratio $4:1:0$. What is the adenylate energy charge? (one decimal)
cards.body:
0.9

Energy charge $= \frac{[\mathrm{ATP}] + \tfrac12[\mathrm{ADP}]}{[\mathrm{ATP}] + [\mathrm{ADP}] + [\mathrm{AMP}]} = \frac{4 + 0.5}{5} = 0.9$.

Why: the cell holds it near $0.8$ to $0.95$; adenylate kinase ($\ce{2ADP <=> ATP + AMP}$) converts falling ATP into a larger relative rise in AMP, which signals low energy.
Key idea: ATP-using pathways slow down and ATP-making ones speed up as the charge falls.
cards.searchQuery: adenylate energy charge formula ATP ADP AMP

cards.title: Why does hydrolysis of ATP to AMP + PP$_i$ drive biosynthetic reactions so strongly?
cards.body:
Inorganic pyrophosphatase hydrolyzes PP$_i$ to 2 P$_i$ ($\Delta G^{\circ\prime} \approx -19\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$), which keeps $[\mathrm{PP_i}]$ low and makes the overall step essentially **irreversible**.

The cell effectively spends two high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds.

Example: fatty acid activation, amino acid activation and DNA polymerization all use this trick.
Watch out: for ATP $\to$ AMP + PP$_i$ people count it as costing 2 ATP equivalents.
cards.searchQuery: ATP to AMP pyrophosphate pyrophosphatase irreversible biosynthesis

cards.title: What is the net equation of glycolysis, from glucose to pyruvate, including the carriers?
cards.body:
$\ce{Glucose + 2NAD+ + 2ADP + 2P_i -> 2 pyruvate + 2NADH + 2H+ + 2ATP + 2H2O}$

Two ATP are spent early and four are made later, so the net gain is $2\,\mathrm{ATP}$.

Why: the $\ce{NADH}$ must be reoxidized (by the electron transport chain, or by fermentation) or glycolysis stalls from lack of $\ce{NAD+}$.
cards.searchQuery: glycolysis net equation glucose 2 pyruvate 2 ATP 2 NADH

cards.title: What regulates hexokinase, the enzyme that traps glucose in most tissues as glucose 6-phosphate?
cards.body:
**Product inhibition** by glucose 6-phosphate.

Hexokinase also has a low $K_m$ for glucose (about $0.1\,\mathrm{mM}$), so it works near saturation even when blood glucose is low.

Why: if downstream steps slow, G6P builds up and shuts off more glucose entering glycolysis.
Watch out: this contrasts with liver glucokinase, which is not inhibited by G6P.
cards.searchQuery: hexokinase product inhibition glucose 6-phosphate low Km

cards.title: Which liver and pancreatic $\beta$-cell isozyme phosphorylates glucose only when blood glucose is high ($K_m \approx 10\,\mathrm{mM}$)?
cards.body:
Glucokinase (hexokinase IV)

Its high $K_m$ and sigmoidal kinetics mean its rate tracks blood glucose after a meal. It is not inhibited by G6P, but a regulatory protein sequesters it in the nucleus when glucose is low.

Why: this lets the liver take up and store glucose only when there is excess, and lets the $\beta$-cell sense glucose to release insulin.
Example: loss-of-function mutations in glucokinase cause MODY2 diabetes.
cards.searchQuery: glucokinase liver high Km hexokinase IV blood glucose sensor

cards.title: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis: fructose 6-phosphate + ATP $\to$ fructose 1,6-bisphosphate + ADP?
cards.body:
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)

It is the most important control point of glycolysis because the product, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, is committed to the glycolytic pathway (G6P can still enter the pentose phosphate pathway or glycogen).

Key idea: its reaction is far from equilibrium, with $\Delta G^{\circ\prime} \approx -14\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.
cards.searchQuery: phosphofructokinase-1 committed step glycolysis

cards.title: Which metabolites activate and which inhibit PFK-1?
cards.body:
Activated by **AMP** and **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate**; inhibited by **ATP** and **citrate** (and by low pH in muscle).

Why: ATP is both a substrate and, at high levels, an allosteric inhibitor that lowers the enzyme's affinity for F6P; AMP reverses that.
Example: citrate signals plenty of biosynthetic precursors and ATP from the citric acid cycle.
Tip: remember ATP and citrate say "enough energy" (inhibit); AMP says "low energy" (activate).
cards.searchQuery: PFK-1 allosteric regulation AMP fructose 2,6-bisphosphate ATP citrate

cards.title: How do insulin and glucagon change the level of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) in the liver?
cards.body:
Insulin **raises** it; glucagon **lowers** it.

The bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2 makes and breaks F2,6BP. Glucagon $\to$ cAMP $\to$ PKA phosphorylation favors the phosphatase (FBPase-2) activity, so F2,6BP falls.

Why: F2,6BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, so a fall turns glycolysis off and gluconeogenesis on.
Key idea: this is a **reciprocal** control of the two opposing pathways.
cards.searchQuery: fructose 2,6-bisphosphate PFK-2 FBPase-2 glucagon insulin liver

cards.title: Which enzyme splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate?
cards.body:
Aldolase

It reverses an aldol condensation. In animal class I aldolases a lysine forms a Schiff base with the ketose.

Why: triose phosphate isomerase then converts DHAP to G3P, so one glucose gives **two** G3P and the rest of glycolysis runs twice.
Watch out: this reaction has a positive standard free energy but proceeds because G3P is removed rapidly.
cards.searchQuery: aldolase fructose 1,6-bisphosphate DHAP glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate

cards.title: Which glycolytic enzyme makes the first NADH, converting glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate with $\mathrm{P_i}$?
cards.body:
Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)

A cysteine thiol attacks the aldehyde; oxidation by $\ce{NAD+}$ gives an energy-rich thioester, which phosphorolysis converts to the acyl phosphate.

Why: this is oxidation coupled to phosphorylation of an inorganic phosphate, without ATP.
Watch out: arsenate can substitute for $\mathrm{P_i}$, giving an unstable product that hydrolyzes at once and so skipping ATP formation at the next step.
cards.searchQuery: GAPDH glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase NADH 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate

cards.title: Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers a phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP. What type of ATP synthesis is this?
cards.body:
Substrate-level phosphorylation

The high-energy acyl phosphate of 1,3-BPG ($\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ of hydrolysis about $-49\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$) pays for making ATP directly, without a proton gradient.

Why: because two 1,3-BPG form per glucose, this step makes $2$ ATP and exactly repays the $2$ ATP spent in the investment phase.
Key idea: the reaction is readily reversible, and gluconeogenesis uses the same enzyme.
cards.searchQuery: phosphoglycerate kinase substrate-level phosphorylation 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate

cards.title: Which glycolytic enzyme dehydrates 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate and is inhibited by fluoride?
cards.body:
Enolase

Removing water traps the phosphate in an enol form, raising its phosphoryl transfer potential from about $-17\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ (2-PG) to $-62$ (PEP).

Example: fluoride is added to blood collection tubes to stop glycolysis in the sample.
Key idea: this is not an oxidation; the energy is **redistributed within the molecule**.
cards.searchQuery: enolase 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate fluoride inhibition

cards.title: How is liver pyruvate kinase regulated by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, ATP, alanine and glucagon?
cards.body:
F1,6BP **activates** (feed-forward); ATP and alanine **inhibit**; glucagon-driven phosphorylation by PKA **inactivates** it.

Why: F1,6BP from PFK-1 says glycolytic flux is running, while alanine and ATP say there is no need for more.
Example: shutting off liver pyruvate kinase in fasting lets PEP flow into gluconeogenesis rather than back to pyruvate.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate kinase regulation fructose 1,6-bisphosphate alanine glucagon phosphorylation

cards.title: Which three glycolytic reactions are essentially irreversible and must be bypassed in gluconeogenesis?
cards.body:
Hexokinase (or glucokinase), phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase.

Each has a large negative $\Delta G$ in the cell, while the other seven steps operate near equilibrium and are shared with gluconeogenesis.

Key idea: the bypass enzymes are pyruvate carboxylase and PEPCK, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose 6-phosphatase.
cards.searchQuery: three irreversible steps glycolysis hexokinase PFK-1 pyruvate kinase

cards.title: What is the metabolic purpose of lactate dehydrogenase in anaerobic muscle?
cards.body:
It regenerates $\ce{NAD+}$ so that glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase can keep running.

$\ce{Pyruvate + NADH + H+ <=> lactate + NAD+}$

Why: without $\ce{NAD+}$, glycolysis, the only ATP source when oxygen is short, would halt.
Watch out: LDH makes no ATP; it only recycles $\ce{NAD+}$ so the ATP of glycolysis can continue.
cards.searchQuery: lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ anaerobic glycolysis

cards.title: Which coenzyme does pyruvate decarboxylase need to convert pyruvate to acetaldehyde in yeast?
cards.body:
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)

TPP, from vitamin $\mathrm{B_1}$, stabilizes the carbanion formed on decarboxylation. Alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol with NADH.

Why: this is the same cofactor class used by pyruvate dehydrogenase, $\alpha$-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase.
Watch out: animals lack pyruvate decarboxylase, so they cannot ferment glucose to ethanol.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate decarboxylase thiamine pyrophosphate yeast ethanol

cards.title: Classic galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of which enzyme of the Leloir pathway?
cards.body:
Galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT)

GALT swaps UMP from UDP-glucose onto galactose 1-phosphate, giving UDP-galactose and glucose 1-phosphate.

Why: galactose 1-phosphate accumulates and is toxic; galactitol builds up and causes cataracts.
Example: infants fail to thrive after drinking milk, so they are treated with a galactose-free diet.
cards.searchQuery: classic galactosemia GALT deficiency Leloir pathway

cards.title: Why does fructose enter glycolysis faster than glucose in the liver?
cards.body:
Fructokinase makes fructose 1-phosphate and aldolase B splits it to DHAP and glyceraldehyde, which bypasses the PFK-1 control point.

So fructose is not regulated by the energy state of the cell, and heavy intake can overload lipogenesis.

Example: **hereditary fructose intolerance** (aldolase B deficiency) traps phosphate as fructose 1-phosphate, causing hypoglycemia and liver damage.
cards.searchQuery: fructose metabolism liver fructokinase aldolase B bypasses PFK-1

cards.title: Which biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate and is activated by acetyl-CoA?
cards.body:
Pyruvate carboxylase

$\ce{Pyruvate + HCO3- + ATP -> oxaloacetate + ADP + P_i}$

Why: high acetyl-CoA (as in fasting, when fat is oxidized) both turns on this enzyme and shuts down pyruvate dehydrogenase, directing pyruvate toward glucose.
Key idea: it is also an **anaplerotic** reaction that refills citric acid cycle intermediates.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate carboxylase biotin acetyl-CoA activation gluconeogenesis

cards.title: Which enzyme converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, using GTP and releasing $\ce{CO2}$?
cards.body:
PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK)

$\ce{OAA + GTP -> PEP + CO2 + GDP}$

The $\ce{CO2}$ added by pyruvate carboxylase is removed here, so the pair drives the unfavorable conversion of pyruvate to PEP.
Why: PEPCK exists in mitochondria and the cytosol; PEPCK transcription is induced by glucagon and cortisol.
cards.searchQuery: PEPCK phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase oxaloacetate GTP gluconeogenesis

cards.title: Which enzyme reverses the PFK-1 step in gluconeogenesis, hydrolyzing fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to fructose 6-phosphate?
cards.body:
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1)

It is inhibited by **AMP** and by **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate**, the same molecules that activate PFK-1.

Key idea: the reciprocal regulation prevents a **futile cycle** in which ATP is burned by both enzymes at once.
cards.searchQuery: fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase gluconeogenesis AMP fructose 2,6-bisphosphate inhibition

cards.title: Which enzyme, found in the ER lumen of the liver and kidney, releases free glucose in the last step of gluconeogenesis?
cards.body:
Glucose 6-phosphatase

It hydrolyzes G6P to glucose and $\mathrm{P_i}$, so the cell can export glucose into the blood.

Why: muscle lacks this enzyme, so muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose.
Example: in von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disease), G6Pase deficiency causes severe fasting hypoglycemia and a large liver.
cards.searchQuery: glucose 6-phosphatase liver kidney ER von Gierke disease

cards.title: How many ATP equivalents (ATP + GTP) does it cost to make one glucose from two pyruvate, counting only the nucleotide triphosphates? (number only)
cards.body:
6

Two pyruvate carboxylase steps use $2$ ATP, two PEPCK steps use $2$ GTP and two phosphoglycerate kinase steps (in reverse) use $2$ ATP.

Compare: glycolysis nets only $2$ ATP, so the cycle between glucose and pyruvate is strongly net negative in energy.
Why: this difference ($6$ vs $2$) is what makes the pathway irreversible overall.
cards.searchQuery: gluconeogenesis energy cost 6 ATP equivalents per glucose

cards.title: What is the Cori cycle?
cards.body:
Muscle makes lactate by glycolysis; the blood carries it to the liver, which turns it back into glucose by gluconeogenesis and returns it to the muscle.

The liver spends $6$ ATP equivalents to make a glucose that gives the muscle only $2$ ATP.

Why: it moves the metabolic burden of lactate and some of the ATP cost from muscle to the liver, which has oxygen to spare.
Compare: the **glucose-alanine cycle** does similar work and also carries amino nitrogen to the liver.
cards.searchQuery: Cori cycle lactate muscle liver gluconeogenesis

cards.title: How many distinct coenzymes does the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex use (TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD, NAD$^+$)? (number only)
cards.body:
5

E1 (pyruvate dehydrogenase) uses **TPP**, E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase) uses **lipoamide** and **CoA**, and E3 (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) uses **FAD** and $\ce{NAD+}$.

Mnemonic: "Tender Loving Care For Nancy": TPP, Lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD.
Key idea: the $\alpha$-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex uses the same five, with its own E1 and E2.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate dehydrogenase complex five coenzymes E1 E2 E3

cards.title: How is the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex turned off by phosphorylation, and what turns that on?
cards.body:
**PDH kinase** phosphorylates E1 and inactivates it; **PDH phosphatase** reverses this.

Kinase is activated by ATP, acetyl-CoA and NADH, and inhibited by pyruvate and ADP. The phosphatase is stimulated by $\ce{Ca^2+}$ and, in some tissues, by insulin.

Why: plenty of ATP and acetyl-CoA means the cell can spare pyruvate for gluconeogenesis or fat synthesis.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase phosphatase regulation acetyl-CoA NADH

cards.title: Why can animals not convert fatty acids (even-chain) into glucose?
cards.body:
The pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot go back to pyruvate.

Each turn of the citric acid cycle also releases two $\ce{CO2}$ for each two carbons entering as acetyl-CoA, so there is no net carbon for oxaloacetate.

Why: plants and bacteria can, using the **glyoxylate cycle**.
Watch out: glycerol and odd-chain fatty acids (propionyl-CoA) can supply glucose carbons.
cards.searchQuery: animals cannot convert fatty acids to glucose pyruvate dehydrogenase irreversible

cards.title: Why do thiamine deficiency (beriberi) and arsenite poisoning both impair pyruvate dehydrogenase?
cards.body:
Thiamine is needed to make TPP, and arsenite binds the **dithiol** of reduced lipoamide.

Either block lets pyruvate build up and be diverted to lactate, causing lactic acidosis, mainly in the nervous system and heart that rely on glucose oxidation.

Example: alcohol use disorder, with poor intake of thiamine, leads to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
cards.searchQuery: thiamine deficiency beriberi arsenite pyruvate dehydrogenase lipoamide

cards.title: Which enzyme condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate in the first step of the citric acid cycle?
cards.body:
Citrate synthase

It has a large negative $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ (about $-32\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$), which pulls the cycle forward and also drives malate dehydrogenase, which is unfavorable by itself.

Why: it is inhibited by ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA and citrate, and its rate depends on the available oxaloacetate.
cards.searchQuery: citrate synthase first step citric acid cycle acetyl-CoA oxaloacetate

cards.title: Which enzyme isomerizes citrate to isocitrate through cis-aconitate and is blocked by fluorocitrate?
cards.body:
Aconitase

It contains an $\ce{Fe-S}$ cluster that binds citrate. The enzyme moves the hydroxyl group from C3 to C2.

Why: citrate is a tertiary alcohol and cannot be oxidized directly, so it is isomerized to the secondary alcohol isocitrate first.
Example: fluoroacetate is converted by the cell to fluorocitrate, which blocks aconitase; this "lethal synthesis" makes it a potent poison.
cards.searchQuery: aconitase citrate to isocitrate fluorocitrate inhibition

cards.title: Which citric acid cycle enzyme makes the first NADH and the first $\ce{CO2}$, converting isocitrate to $\alpha$-ketoglutarate?
cards.body:
Isocitrate dehydrogenase

It is a major control point: **ADP** and $\ce{Ca^2+}$ activate it; **ATP** and **NADH** inhibit it.

Why: the cycle speeds up when energy is needed and slows when the cell is energy-rich.
Watch out: the mitochondrial form uses $\ce{NAD+}$; the cytosolic and peroxisomal forms use $\ce{NADP+}$ and supply NADPH.
cards.searchQuery: isocitrate dehydrogenase regulation ADP ATP NADH citric acid cycle

cards.title: Which citric acid cycle enzyme complex, resembling pyruvate dehydrogenase, converts $\alpha$-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA?
cards.body:
$\alpha$-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex

It uses the same five cofactors as PDH and releases the second $\ce{CO2}$ and the second NADH of the cycle.

Why: it is inhibited by its products **succinyl-CoA** and **NADH**, and by ATP, but unlike PDH it is not regulated by phosphorylation.
cards.searchQuery: alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex succinyl-CoA citric acid cycle

cards.title: Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes which nucleotide triphosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation in most animal tissues?
cards.body:
GTP (some tissues make ATP instead)

The thioester energy of succinyl-CoA drives phosphorylation of the enzyme's histidine, and the phosphate then moves to GDP.

Key idea: this is the cycle's only direct nucleotide triphosphate output, and nucleoside diphosphate kinase can convert GTP to ATP.
cards.searchQuery: succinyl-CoA synthetase GTP substrate-level phosphorylation

cards.title: Which dicarboxylate is a classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase?
cards.body:
Malonate

It resembles succinate but has no CH$_2$-CH$_2$ unit to dehydrogenate, so it binds the active site and blocks it.

Why: succinate dehydrogenase is the only citric acid cycle enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane; it is **Complex II** of the electron transport chain, with covalently bound FAD.
Key idea: it makes $\ce{FADH2}$ rather than NADH.
cards.searchQuery: malonate competitive inhibitor succinate dehydrogenase complex II

cards.title: Malate dehydrogenase has a large positive $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ ($+29.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$). Why does it still run forward in the cycle?
cards.body:
The next enzyme, citrate synthase, consumes oxaloacetate in a very favorable reaction, keeping $[\mathrm{OAA}]$ extremely low.

Why: a low product concentration makes $Q$ small, so the actual $\Delta G$ is near zero or negative.
Key idea: this is an example of an unfavorable step **pulled** by a favorable one, as in many metabolic pathways.
Watch out: this is why $[\mathrm{OAA}]$ in the mitochondria is so low (micromolar or lower).
cards.searchQuery: malate dehydrogenase positive delta G pulled by citrate synthase oxaloacetate

cards.title: How many NADH are produced in one turn of the citric acid cycle (per acetyl-CoA)? (number only)
cards.body:
3

One turn also gives $1\,\ce{FADH2}$, $1$ GTP (or ATP) and $2\,\ce{CO2}$.

Why: the NADH come from isocitrate dehydrogenase, $\alpha$-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase; $\ce{FADH2}$ from succinate dehydrogenase.
Tip: per glucose, double everything the cycle gives: $6$ NADH, $2$ $\ce{FADH2}$ and $2$ GTP.
cards.searchQuery: citric acid cycle products per turn 3 NADH 1 FADH2 1 GTP

cards.title: In a single turn of the cycle, do the two $\ce{CO2}$ released come from the entering acetyl group?
cards.body:
No. They come from the oxaloacetate-derived carbons; the acetyl carbons become part of the 4-carbon intermediates.

The acetyl carbons are released as $\ce{CO2}$ only in later turns, because succinate is symmetric and scrambles the two ends.

Why: succinate is symmetric, so the two ends of the 4-carbon unit are scrambled and acetyl-derived carbons can be lost in later turns.
cards.searchQuery: citric acid cycle carbon fate acetyl CoA carbons released later turns CO2

cards.title: What do "anaplerotic" reactions do for the citric acid cycle?
cards.body:
They **replenish** intermediates that are withdrawn for biosynthesis.

The main one is pyruvate carboxylase ($\text{pyruvate} \to \text{oxaloacetate}$); glutamate dehydrogenase and transaminases supply $\alpha$-ketoglutarate, and propionyl-CoA gives succinyl-CoA.

Why: the cycle is **amphibolic**; citrate goes to fatty acids, $\alpha$-KG and OAA to amino acids, succinyl-CoA to heme. Without refilling, the cycle would stall.
cards.searchQuery: anaplerotic reactions citric acid cycle replenish intermediates amphibolic

cards.title: Which enzyme of the glyoxylate cycle cleaves isocitrate into succinate and glyoxylate, bypassing the $\ce{CO2}$-releasing steps?
cards.body:
Isocitrate lyase

Malate synthase then joins glyoxylate with a second acetyl-CoA to form malate.

Why: in plant seeds and some bacteria, this lets two acetyl-CoA make one net 4-carbon unit, so fats can be converted to carbohydrate.
Watch out: animals lack isocitrate lyase and malate synthase.
cards.searchQuery: glyoxylate cycle isocitrate lyase malate synthase plants

cards.title: What is the stereochemical hallmark of the fumarase reaction in the citric acid cycle?
cards.body:
It adds water across the trans double bond of fumarate to give only **L-malate**.

The enzyme is stereospecific: it never makes D-malate, and it uses the same active site in both directions.

Key idea: the sequence succinate $\to$ fumarate $\to$ malate $\to$ oxaloacetate is the same dehydrogenation, hydration, dehydrogenation logic that fatty acid $\beta$-oxidation uses.
cards.searchQuery: fumarase fumarate to L-malate stereospecific hydration

cards.title: Which classic inhibitor of Complex I (NADH-Q oxidoreductase) blocks electron transfer to ubiquinone?
cards.body:
Rotenone

Complex I passes electrons from NADH through FMN and a chain of $\ce{Fe-S}$ clusters to ubiquinone, and pumps $4\,\ce{H+}$ per electron pair.

Example: rotenone is a plant-derived insecticide and fish poison; with Complex I blocked, NADH-linked oxidation stops but succinate can still feed in at Complex II.
cards.searchQuery: rotenone complex I inhibitor NADH-Q oxidoreductase

cards.title: Does Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) pump protons?
cards.body:
No

It passes electrons from succinate through FAD and $\ce{Fe-S}$ clusters to ubiquinone, but the free energy change is too small to drive proton pumping.

Why: because $\ce{FADH2}$ electrons enter at Q and skip Complex I, they support fewer protons pumped, so they give less ATP than NADH.
Watch out: this is why FADH2-linked oxidation yields about $1.5$ ATP versus $2.5$ for NADH.
cards.searchQuery: complex II succinate dehydrogenase does not pump protons FADH2

cards.title: Which inhibitor blocks Complex III (cytochrome $bc_1$) at the $Q_i$ site?
cards.body:
Antimycin A

Complex III oxidizes ubiquinol and reduces cytochrome $c$ through the **Q cycle**, which releases $4\,\ce{H+}$ on the intermembrane side per net $\mathrm{QH_2}$ oxidized, while $2\,\ce{H+}$ are taken from the matrix.

Why: its cytochromes and Rieske $\ce{Fe-S}$ center are one-electron carriers, while Q can carry two, so the Q cycle splits the flow.
cards.searchQuery: antimycin A complex III inhibitor Q cycle cytochrome bc1

cards.title: Which poison binds the heme $a_3$-$\ce{Cu_B}$ center of cytochrome $c$ oxidase and stops electron flow to oxygen?
cards.body:
Cyanide (also CO and azide)

Complex IV transfers four electrons from cytochrome $c$ to $\ce{O2}$ to form $2\,\ce{H2O}$ and pumps protons: $4\,\mathrm{cyt}\,c_{red} + 4\,\ce{H+} + \ce{O2} \to 4\,\mathrm{cyt}\,c_{ox} + 2\,\ce{H2O}$.

Why: oxygen is reduced fully to water without releasing partially reduced intermediates (superoxide, peroxide) because all four electrons are delivered at one site.
cards.searchQuery: cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase complex IV heme a3

cards.title: Which mobile, lipid-soluble carrier shuttles electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III?
cards.body:
Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q, $\mathrm{Q}$)

Its isoprenoid tail keeps it in the inner membrane, and it can carry two electrons and two protons as $\mathrm{QH_2}$, passing through the semiquinone radical.

Compare: cytochrome $c$ is the mobile **water-soluble** carrier between Complexes III and IV, carrying one electron at a time.
cards.searchQuery: ubiquinone coenzyme Q mobile electron carrier electron transport chain

cards.title: What is the order of electron carriers from NADH to oxygen in the mitochondrial chain?
cards.body:
NADH $\to$ Complex I $\to$ Q $\to$ Complex III $\to$ cytochrome $c$ $\to$ Complex IV $\to$ $\ce{O2}$

Succinate enters through Complex II, which feeds Q; glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and the fatty acyl-CoA dehydrogenase ETF pathway also feed Q.

Key idea: electrons always flow toward carriers with higher (more positive) reduction potentials.
cards.searchQuery: electron transport chain order complex I Q complex III cytochrome c complex IV

cards.title: About how many protons are pumped per NADH (and per succinate) as electrons travel through the chain to $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
About $10\,\ce{H+}$ per NADH and $6\,\ce{H+}$ per succinate (per $\ce{FADH2}$).

Complex I pumps $4$, Complex III $4$ (net, via the Q cycle) and Complex IV $2$ per electron pair.

Why: succinate skips Complex I, so it loses $4$ protons.
Watch out: textbooks differ somewhat in these counts, so always use the numbers your course gives you.
cards.searchQuery: protons pumped per NADH 10 per FADH2 6 electron transport chain

cards.title: Where is cytochrome $c$ located, and what else does it do besides carrying electrons?
cards.body:
It is a small soluble protein loosely bound to the outer face of the **inner membrane**, in the intermembrane space.

When released into the cytosol it helps assemble the apoptosome with Apaf-1, which activates caspase-9 and begins apoptosis.

Why: its heme iron cycles between $\ce{Fe^3+}$ and $\ce{Fe^2+}$, one electron at a time.
cards.searchQuery: cytochrome c intermembrane space electron carrier apoptosis release

cards.title: What does Boyer's binding-change mechanism propose for ATP synthase?
cards.body:
The three $\beta$ subunits of $\mathrm{F_1}$ cycle through three conformations (**loose, tight, open**) as the central $\gamma$ shaft rotates, driven by proton flow through $\mathrm{F_o}$.

The energy is used mainly to **release** the tightly bound ATP, not to form it.

Why: ATP forms spontaneously in the tight site, where the enzyme holds ADP and $\mathrm{P_i}$ in just the right position.
Key idea: rotation has been directly observed under the microscope.
cards.searchQuery: Boyer binding change mechanism ATP synthase rotation beta subunits

cards.title: Using the common textbook count, how many protons must flow in per ATP made and exported to the cytosol? (number only)
cards.body:
4

About $3\,\ce{H+}$ pass through ATP synthase (the $\mathrm{F_o}$ ring has $8$ c subunits in mammals, so $8/3 \approx 2.7$), plus $1\,\ce{H+}$ for the phosphate carrier that brings $\mathrm{P_i}$ in.

Why: with $10\,\ce{H+}$ pumped per NADH, $10/4 = 2.5$ ATP per NADH; with $6$ per $\ce{FADH2}$, $6/4 = 1.5$.
cards.searchQuery: protons per ATP 4 ATP synthase c ring phosphate carrier

cards.title: What is the currently used P/O ratio (ATP per oxygen atom) for NADH oxidized through the full chain? (number only)
cards.body:
2.5

For $\ce{FADH2}$ the value is $1.5$. Older textbooks used $3$ and $2$, giving the figures of $36$ to $38$ ATP per glucose.

Watch out: the P/O ratio is not a whole number, because proton pumping and ATP synthesis are coupled through a gradient and not through a chemical intermediate.
cards.searchQuery: P/O ratio NADH 2.5 FADH2 1.5 oxidative phosphorylation

cards.title: Using P/O ratios of $2.5$ (NADH) and $1.5$ ($\ce{FADH2}$) and the malate-aspartate shuttle, how many ATP does complete oxidation of one glucose give? (number only)
cards.body:
32

Glycolysis: $2$ ATP + $2$ NADH ($5$) = $7$. Pyruvate dehydrogenase: $2$ NADH = $5$. Citric acid cycle: $6$ NADH ($15$) + $2\,\ce{FADH2}$ ($3$) + $2$ GTP ($2$) = $20$.

Total: $7 + 5 + 20 = 32$.
Watch out: with the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle, the two cytosolic NADH count as $\ce{FADH2}$ ($3$ instead of $5$), giving $30$; older texts say $36$ or $38$.
cards.searchQuery: ATP yield per glucose 32 aerobic respiration P/O 2.5 1.5

cards.title: Which shuttle moves reducing equivalents into the matrix as $\ce{FADH2}$ (in muscle and brain), costing some ATP yield?
cards.body:
The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle

Cytosolic glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase uses NADH; the mitochondrial isozyme (in the inner membrane) passes electrons to Q, so they enter at the level of $\ce{FADH2}$.

Compare: the **malate-aspartate shuttle** (liver, heart) delivers NADH to the matrix at full value, but depends on the membrane potential.
cards.searchQuery: glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle vs malate aspartate shuttle FADH2

cards.title: Which protein in brown fat mitochondria dissipates the proton gradient as heat instead of making ATP?
cards.body:
Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1, thermogenin)

It lets protons leak back into the matrix, so electron transport runs without ATP synthesis, and the energy is released as heat.

Example: newborns and hibernating animals use it for non-shivering thermogenesis; the chemical uncoupler 2,4-dinitrophenol acts the same way and is dangerous.
cards.searchQuery: UCP1 thermogenin brown fat uncoupling protein heat

cards.title: Which antibiotic blocks the $\mathrm{F_o}$ proton channel of ATP synthase?
cards.body:
Oligomycin

With $\mathrm{F_o}$ blocked, protons cannot re-enter; the gradient builds up and electron transport slows dramatically.

Why: this shows **tight coupling**: oxygen consumption depends on ATP synthesis. An uncoupler such as DNP restores oxygen use despite oligomycin.
cards.searchQuery: oligomycin ATP synthase Fo inhibitor respiratory control

cards.title: What is respiratory (acceptor) control?
cards.body:
The rate of oxygen consumption is set by the availability of **ADP**.

When ATP use is low, ADP falls, ATP synthase slows, the proton gradient builds up and electron transport is held back; when work raises ADP, the chain speeds up.

Why: the ADP/ATP translocase brings ADP into the matrix in exchange for ATP, driven by the membrane potential, so the cytosolic ADP/ATP ratio signals demand.
cards.searchQuery: respiratory control ADP availability oxygen consumption ATP synthase

cards.title: Which enzyme converts superoxide ($\ce{O2^{.-}}$), leaked from the electron transport chain, into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen?
cards.body:
Superoxide dismutase (SOD)

$\ce{2O2^{.-} + 2H+ -> H2O2 + O2}$

Catalase or glutathione peroxidase then converts $\ce{H2O2}$ to water.

Why: a small percent of electrons leak to $\ce{O2}$ at Complexes I and III, and unchecked reactive oxygen species damage DNA, proteins and lipids.
cards.searchQuery: superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide mitochondria

cards.title: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the pentose phosphate pathway, controlled by the $\ce{NADP+}/\mathrm{NADPH}$ ratio?
cards.body:
Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)

$\ce{G6P + NADP+ -> 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH + H+}$

It is strongly inhibited by NADPH, so the pathway runs only when the cell needs NADPH (high $\ce{NADP+}$).

Why: insulin raises G6PD expression in the liver, supporting fatty acid synthesis.
cards.searchQuery: glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase rate limiting pentose phosphate pathway NADPH

cards.title: How many NADPH are made per glucose 6-phosphate that passes through the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway? (number only)
cards.body:
2

$\ce{G6P + 2NADP+ + H2O -> ribulose 5-phosphate + CO2 + 2NADPH + 2H+}$

The two oxidations are G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase; the latter also releases $\ce{CO2}$.

Key idea: ribulose 5-phosphate is then isomerized to ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotides.
cards.searchQuery: pentose phosphate pathway oxidative phase 2 NADPH ribulose 5-phosphate CO2

cards.title: Which TPP-dependent enzyme of the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway transfers two-carbon units between sugars?
cards.body:
Transketolase

Compare: transaldolase moves three-carbon units and needs no cofactor (it forms a Schiff base with lysine).

Why: together they recycle pentoses into fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, so the cell can make ribose or convert it back to glycolytic intermediates as needed.
Example: red cell transketolase activity is used as a clinical test for thiamine deficiency.
cards.searchQuery: transketolase TPP pentose phosphate pathway non-oxidative two carbon transfer

cards.title: Why does G6PD deficiency cause hemolytic anemia after fava beans or primaquine?
cards.body:
Red cells have no other NADPH source, and NADPH keeps **glutathione** reduced.

Without enough reduced glutathione, oxidants (from fava beans, primaquine, infection) damage hemoglobin and membranes, and the cells lyse.

Why: it is X-linked and the most common human enzyme deficiency; it also gives some protection against malaria.
Key idea: the failure is in antioxidant defense, not in energy supply.
cards.searchQuery: G6PD deficiency hemolytic anemia fava beans glutathione NADPH

cards.title: Why does the cell keep NADPH and NADH in different redox states?
cards.body:
The cytosolic $\ce{NADP+}/\mathrm{NADPH}$ pool is kept **highly reduced** (NADPH high) for biosynthesis, while $\ce{NAD+}/\mathrm{NADH}$ is kept **oxidized** (NAD$^+$ high) for catabolism.

Example: NADPH drives fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and glutathione reduction; NAD$^+$ accepts electrons in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.

Why: enzymes use the extra 2'-phosphate to tell the two apart.
cards.searchQuery: NADPH vs NADH redox state biosynthesis catabolism cytosol

cards.title: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose 1-phosphate from glycogen. What cofactor does it need, and what does it use as the second substrate?
cards.body:
Cofactor: **pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)**. Second substrate: inorganic phosphate ($\mathrm{P_i}$), not ATP.

It cleaves $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$ links by **phosphorolysis**, working from the non-reducing ends, and stops four residues short of a branch point.

Why: phosphorolysis saves the ATP that hydrolysis and re-phosphorylation would cost.
Key idea: the products are glucose 1-phosphate, which phosphoglucomutase converts to G6P.
cards.searchQuery: glycogen phosphorylase pyridoxal phosphate phosphorolysis glucose 1-phosphate

cards.title: How does the debranching enzyme clear a branch point after phosphorylase stops?
cards.body:
A **transferase** moves three of the four remaining residues to another chain end, and an $\alpha(1\rightarrow6)$-**glucosidase** then hydrolyzes the last residue, releasing free glucose.

So about $10\%$ of glycogen's glucose is released as free glucose rather than glucose 1-phosphate.

Why: the two activities sit on one bifunctional protein.
cards.searchQuery: glycogen debranching enzyme transferase alpha 1,6 glucosidase

cards.title: Which activated sugar donates glucose to the growing glycogen chain, and which enzyme adds it?
cards.body:
**UDP-glucose**, added by **glycogen synthase** to a non-reducing end by an $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$ link.

UDP-glucose comes from glucose 1-phosphate + UTP (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase), and pyrophosphate hydrolysis makes this step irreversible.

Watch out: synthase needs a primer; glycogenin starts a chain by self-glucosylation on a tyrosine.
cards.searchQuery: glycogen synthase UDP-glucose glycogenin primer synthesis

cards.title: How do glucagon and epinephrine versus insulin control glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase?
cards.body:
Glucagon and epinephrine: $\text{cAMP} \to \text{PKA} \to \text{phosphorylase kinase} \to$ **phosphorylase a** (active), while PKA also phosphorylates and **inactivates** glycogen synthase.

Insulin activates protein phosphatase 1 and inhibits GSK3, so synthase is dephosphorylated and **active** and phosphorylase is inactive.

Key idea: the two enzymes are reciprocally controlled, so glycogen is never built and broken at the same time.
cards.searchQuery: glycogen phosphorylase synthase regulation cAMP PKA insulin phosphatase

cards.title: How does the purpose of glycogen breakdown differ between liver and muscle?
cards.body:
Liver releases free glucose to keep **blood glucose** steady (it has glucose 6-phosphatase); muscle burns glucose 6-phosphate for **its own** ATP and lacks that enzyme.

Muscle phosphorylase $b$ is also activated by AMP and $\ce{Ca^2+}$ (via phosphorylase kinase) during exercise; liver phosphorylase responds to glucagon and is inhibited by glucose.

Why: muscle responds to epinephrine, but not to glucagon, which it lacks receptors for.
cards.searchQuery: liver vs muscle glycogen function glucose 6-phosphatase AMP phosphorylase

cards.title: Which glycogen storage disease is caused by deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase, causing exercise intolerance and painful cramps?
cards.body:
McArdle disease (type V)

Muscle glycogen builds up, but cannot be mobilized, so exercise causes cramping and fatigue, and blood lactate does not rise during ischemic exercise.

Compare: **Pompe disease** (type II) is lysosomal $\alpha$-glucosidase deficiency, and **von Gierke disease** (type I) is glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency.
cards.searchQuery: McArdle disease type V muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency

cards.title: How many ATP equivalents are spent to add one glucose residue (starting from glucose 6-phosphate) to glycogen? (number only)
cards.body:
1

UTP is spent making UDP-glucose and is regenerated from ATP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase, so the net cost is one ATP per glucose residue. Hydrolysis of the released $\mathrm{PP_i}$ makes the step irreversible without costing extra ATP.

Why: about $3\%$ of the energy in a stored glucose is spent storing it, so glycogen is a very efficient fuel store.
Watch out: some courses count the $\mathrm{PP_i}$ hydrolysis as a second ATP equivalent; check your course's convention.
cards.searchQuery: energy cost glycogen synthesis ATP equivalent per glucose UTP

cards.title: Activating a fatty acid to fatty acyl-CoA consumes how many ATP equivalents? (number only)
cards.body:
2

$\ce{RCOO- + CoA + ATP -> RCO-CoA + AMP + PP_i}$, followed by pyrophosphatase hydrolyzing the $\mathrm{PP_i}$.

Two phosphoanhydride bonds are spent, even though only one ATP molecule is used (it becomes AMP).

Watch out: this is why the net yield of palmitate is $108 - 2 = 106$ ATP.
cards.searchQuery: fatty acid activation acyl-CoA synthetase ATP to AMP 2 ATP equivalents

cards.title: Which molecule carries long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
cards.body:
Carnitine

CPT-I on the outer membrane makes acylcarnitine, a translocase moves it across the inner membrane, and CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix.

Why: **malonyl-CoA** inhibits CPT-I, so newly made fatty acids (made in the cytosol) are not immediately burned.
Key idea: CPT-I is the rate-limiting, regulated step of fatty acid oxidation.
cards.searchQuery: carnitine shuttle CPT-I malonyl-CoA fatty acid oxidation mitochondria

cards.title: What are the four reactions of each $\beta$-oxidation cycle, in order?
cards.body:
1. Oxidation by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (makes $\ce{FADH2}$)
2. Hydration by enoyl-CoA hydratase
3. Oxidation by L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (makes NADH)
4. Thiolysis by $\beta$-ketothiolase, releasing acetyl-CoA

Why: each round shortens the acyl-CoA by two carbons.
Tip: oxidation, hydration, oxidation, thiolysis. The same logic, run in reverse, builds fatty acids.
cards.searchQuery: beta oxidation four steps acyl-CoA dehydrogenase hydratase thiolase

cards.title: How many rounds of $\beta$-oxidation fully cleave palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) into acetyl-CoA? (number only)
cards.body:
7

The last round cleaves a 4-carbon chain into two acetyl-CoA, so $n/2 - 1 = 7$ rounds give $8$ acetyl-CoA, $7\,\ce{FADH2}$ and $7$ NADH.

Example: for a 12-carbon fatty acid, $12/2 - 1 = 5$ rounds.
cards.searchQuery: palmitate beta oxidation 7 rounds 8 acetyl-CoA

cards.title: Using P/O ratios of $2.5$ and $1.5$, what is the net ATP yield from complete oxidation of one palmitate? (number only)
cards.body:
106

Eight acetyl-CoA give $8 \times 10 = 80$; $7\,\ce{FADH2}$ and $7$ NADH give $7 \times (1.5 + 2.5) = 28$; subtract $2$ for activation.

$80 + 28 - 2 = 106$

Watch out: with the older ratios ($3$ and $2$) the answer is $129$ or $131$ ATP; always state the convention.
cards.searchQuery: ATP yield complete oxidation palmitate 106 ATP

cards.title: Which vitamin-derived cofactor does methylmalonyl-CoA mutase need to convert propionyl-CoA's product into succinyl-CoA?
cards.body:
Vitamin $\mathrm{B_{12}}$ (adenosylcobalamin)

Odd-chain fatty acids end with propionyl-CoA, which is carboxylated (biotin) to methylmalonyl-CoA, racemized and then rearranged to succinyl-CoA by the mutase.

Example: $\mathrm{B_{12}}$ deficiency causes methylmalonic acid to build up, which clinicians use as a diagnostic marker.
cards.searchQuery: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase vitamin B12 propionyl-CoA succinyl-CoA

cards.title: Which mitochondrial enzyme is the rate-limiting step of ketone body synthesis, condensing acetoacetyl-CoA with acetyl-CoA?
cards.body:
HMG-CoA synthase (mitochondrial)

HMG-CoA lyase then cleaves HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA; acetoacetate can be reduced to $\beta$-hydroxybutyrate (NADH-linked) or decarboxylate to acetone.

Why: during fasting, the liver makes more acetyl-CoA from fat than the citric acid cycle can use (low oxaloacetate), so the surplus becomes ketone bodies.
Watch out: the cytosolic isozyme makes HMG-CoA for cholesterol.
cards.searchQuery: HMG-CoA synthase mitochondrial ketogenesis rate-limiting ketone bodies

cards.title: Why can the liver make ketone bodies but not use them?
cards.body:
It lacks **succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase** (thiophorase), which activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA.

Heart, skeletal muscle and (in prolonged fasting) brain have it, so ketone bodies are exported from the liver as fuel.

Why: this keeps liver as a net supplier rather than a competing consumer.
cards.searchQuery: liver cannot use ketone bodies thiophorase succinyl-CoA acetoacetate CoA transferase

cards.title: Which biotin-dependent enzyme catalyzes the committed step of fatty acid synthesis, making malonyl-CoA?
cards.body:
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)

$\ce{Acetyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP -> malonyl-CoA + ADP + P_i}$

It is cytosolic. Malonyl-CoA is the 2-carbon donor for chain elongation and also the CPT-I inhibitor that stops fat burning.

Key idea: this adds one carbon unit, as $\ce{CO2}$, which is later lost again in the condensation.
cards.searchQuery: acetyl-CoA carboxylase committed step fatty acid synthesis malonyl-CoA biotin

cards.title: How is acetyl-CoA carboxylase regulated by citrate, palmitoyl-CoA, insulin, glucagon and AMPK?
cards.body:
**Activated** by citrate and by insulin (via dephosphorylation); **inhibited** by palmitoyl-CoA and by phosphorylation from AMPK or glucagon-induced PKA.

Why: citrate signals plenty of acetyl-CoA and ATP; palmitoyl-CoA is the end product; AMPK signals low energy.
Key idea: the cell never makes and burns fat at once, since ACC also lowers fat oxidation by making malonyl-CoA only when fed.
cards.searchQuery: acetyl-CoA carboxylase regulation citrate palmitoyl-CoA AMPK insulin

cards.title: How many NADPH are used to synthesize one palmitate from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA? (number only)
cards.body:
14

Each of the $7$ elongation cycles uses $2$ NADPH (one for the $\beta$-ketoacyl reduction and one for the enoyl reduction).

Overall: $\ce{8 acetyl-CoA + 7ATP + 14NADPH -> palmitate + 8CoA + 7ADP + 14NADP+ + 6H2O + 7P_i}$.
Why: NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway and from malic enzyme.
cards.searchQuery: palmitate synthesis 14 NADPH fatty acid synthase 7 ATP

cards.title: How does acetyl-CoA leave the mitochondria for fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol?
cards.body:
As **citrate**, which is exported and cleaved by **ATP-citrate lyase** into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate.

The oxaloacetate is reduced to malate and then oxidized by malic enzyme to pyruvate, giving NADPH.

Why: the inner membrane has no acetyl-CoA carrier, and a high citrate level means energy and carbon are in surplus.
cards.searchQuery: citrate shuttle ATP-citrate lyase acetyl-CoA export mitochondria fatty acid synthesis

cards.title: Which cofactor do all transaminases (aminotransferases) use to shuttle amino groups?
cards.body:
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, from vitamin $\mathrm{B_6}$)

The amino group moves from an amino acid to PLP (forming pyridoxamine phosphate), then to an $\alpha$-keto acid, usually $\alpha$-ketoglutarate, giving glutamate.

Example: ALT converts alanine and $\alpha$-KG to pyruvate and glutamate; AST does the same with aspartate and oxaloacetate. Elevated serum levels signal liver injury.
cards.searchQuery: transaminase pyridoxal phosphate PLP amino group transfer ALT AST

cards.title: Which allosteric activator is required by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the regulated first step of the urea cycle?
cards.body:
N-Acetylglutamate (NAG)

$\ce{NH4+ + HCO3- + 2ATP -> carbamoyl phosphate + 2ADP + P_i}$ in the mitochondrial matrix.

Why: arginine stimulates NAG synthesis, so the cycle speeds up when amino acid breakdown increases.
Watch out: CPS II, in the cytosol, makes carbamoyl phosphate for pyrimidines from glutamine and is not NAG-dependent.
cards.searchQuery: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I N-acetylglutamate urea cycle activator

cards.title: Which urea cycle steps occur in the mitochondrial matrix, and which in the cytosol?
cards.body:
**Matrix:** CPS I and ornithine transcarbamoylase (making citrulline). **Cytosol:** argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase.

Citrulline exits and ornithine enters through a transporter.

Example: OTC deficiency, the most common urea cycle defect, is X-linked; carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, so **orotic acid** rises in urine.
cards.searchQuery: urea cycle mitochondria cytosol ornithine transcarbamoylase OTC deficiency orotic acid

cards.title: How many high-energy phosphate bonds (ATP equivalents) does the urea cycle consume per urea made? (number only)
cards.body:
4

CPS I uses $2$ ATP, and argininosuccinate synthetase converts ATP to AMP + PP$_i$, which counts as $2$.

Why: part of the cost is returned, because the fumarate produced can form malate and then NADH in the citric acid cycle.
Key idea: the nitrogens in urea come from $\ce{NH4+}$ and from aspartate.
cards.searchQuery: urea cycle energy cost 4 high-energy phosphate bonds per urea

cards.title: Which two amino acids are purely ketogenic in humans?
cards.body:
Leucine and lysine

Their carbons break down only to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, never to a gluconeogenic intermediate.

Why: acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to net glucose in animals.
Example: Phe, Tyr, Trp, Ile and Thr are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
cards.searchQuery: purely ketogenic amino acids leucine lysine

cards.title: How do insulin and glucagon shift liver metabolism between the fed and fasting states?
cards.body:
**Insulin (fed):** favors glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, fatty acid synthesis and storage. **Glucagon (fasting):** favors glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis through cAMP and PKA.

Why: the main control tool is phosphorylation of key enzymes, with long-term changes in gene expression (PEPCK, G6Pase up with glucagon).
Key idea: the two hormones act reciprocally, so opposing pathways are not active together.
cards.searchQuery: insulin glucagon fed fasting state liver metabolism regulation

cards.title: Which kinase acts as the cell's energy sensor, activated when the AMP/ATP ratio rises?
cards.body:
AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)

Once active, it phosphorylates targets to turn **on** ATP-producing pathways (glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation) and turn **off** ATP-consuming ones (ACC and fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis).

Example: exercise and the drug metformin both activate AMPK.
cards.searchQuery: AMPK energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase metabolism

cards.title: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statin drugs?
cards.body:
HMG-CoA reductase

It converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate using $2$ NADPH. Statins are competitive inhibitors that resemble HMG-CoA.

Why: it is controlled by cholesterol-dependent degradation, SREBP-mediated transcription and AMPK phosphorylation.
Watch out: this is the cytosolic/ER pathway; the mitochondrial HMG-CoA made for ketogenesis is a separate pool.
cards.searchQuery: HMG-CoA reductase rate limiting cholesterol synthesis statins

cards.title: During prolonged fasting, which fuel does the brain increasingly use to spare glucose and body protein?
cards.body:
Ketone bodies ($\beta$-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate)

The brain cannot burn fatty acids, which do not cross the blood-brain barrier well as albumin-bound molecules, but it can oxidize ketone bodies made by the liver.

Why: this reduces the glucose needed from gluconeogenesis, so less muscle protein is broken down.
Example: after several days of fasting, ketones can supply a large share of the brain's energy.
cards.searchQuery: fasting brain uses ketone bodies spare glucose protein
